subject: mathematics
question_text: If A is the matrix with rows (1, 2, 2), (2, 1, 2) and (2, 2, 1), then show that A² − 4A − 5I = O.

mark_split.label: Find A² by multiplying A by itself
Subtract and show the result is O

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Junior Inter Maths-1A (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.54 — SAQ chapter 7 Matrices, answer 43.1, on a ★★★ SSP (Super Scoring Page). Printed appearances: AP 16,17 · TS 17. ⚠ THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S — no [N Marks] tags are printed against this answer (the only SAQ in the chapter that carries them is answer 40 on book p.51, printed 1+1+1+1). recall_prompt: Say how you would show this — say what you have to work out first and what you do with it.

steps.label: Find A²
steps.margin_note: Half the marks. A² means A × A, not each entry squared. Multiply row by column: the top-left entry is row 1 against column 1, which is 1(1) + 2(2) + 2(2) = 9.

recall.must_convey: That A² is A multiplied by itself row against column — NOT each entry squared — giving 9 on the diagonal and 8 elsewhere.
accept: A squared means A times A so multiply row by column and you get nine on the diagonal and eight elsewhere
multiply the matrix by itself using row into column multiplication
find A into A, not the squares of the entries
A square ante A into A, row into column multiply cheyyali
do the matrix multiplication of A with itself to get A squared

steps.why: Squaring a matrix is repeated multiplication, and matrix multiplication is row against column. Squaring the entries one by one gives a completely different matrix and is the single commonest error here.
common_mistakes: Squaring each entry instead of multiplying the matrices.
Stopping after the first row; all nine entries are needed.

steps.label: Write 4A and 5I
steps.margin_note: Third mark. 4A multiplies EVERY entry of A by 4. 5I is 5 down the diagonal and 0 everywhere else — I is the identity matrix, not a matrix of ones.

recall.must_convey: That 4A multiplies every entry of A by 4, and that 5I is 5 on the diagonal with zeros elsewhere.
accept: four A means every entry of A times four and five I is five on the diagonal with zeros elsewhere
multiply A by four entrywise and write five times the identity matrix
write four A and five I where I is the identity
four A ante prathi entry ni four tho multiply, five I ante diagonal lo five
scalar multiply A by four and put five down the diagonal for five I
reject: write four A and five I

steps.why: A number times a matrix multiplies every entry. I is the matrix that leaves any matrix unchanged under multiplication, so it has 1s on the diagonal and 0s elsewhere — that is why 5I is not a grid of 5s.
common_mistakes: Writing 5I as a matrix full of 5s.
Multiplying only the diagonal of A by 4.
Treating I as the matrix of all ones.

steps.label: Subtract and conclude
steps.margin_note: Last mark. Subtract entry by entry. The diagonal gives 9 − 4 − 5 = 0 and every other entry gives 8 − 8 − 0 = 0, so the whole matrix is zero.

recall.must_convey: That the three matrices are subtracted entry by entry and every entry comes out zero, so the result is the zero matrix O.
accept: subtract entry by entry, the diagonal gives nine minus four minus five which is zero and the others give eight minus eight which is zero
take A squared minus four A minus five I and every entry is zero so it is the null matrix
do the subtraction and all nine entries vanish giving O
entry by entry subtract cheste anni zero avthai, so O vasthundi
the result is the zero matrix because each entry cancels

steps.why: O is the ZERO matrix, not the number 0. Writing the full 3×3 of zeros before the conclusion is what shows you know the difference.
common_mistakes: Writing "= 0" instead of "= O" — the answer is a matrix.
Subtracting only the diagonal and assuming the rest.
Dropping the 5I because its off-diagonal entries are zero.
